title: Research Methods in Applied Linguistics and ELT
overview: Research connects a worthwhile question with suitable evidence and a defensible answer. Move from problem and literature to design, participants and instruments, then analysis, interpretation and responsible reporting. Every choice should fit the question.
journey: Find the uncertainty: problem, literature, gap and research questions.
Choose evidence that can answer it: design, sample, instruments and ethics.
Turn evidence into a justified answer: analyse, interpret and acknowledge limitations.
Explain the contribution: report, cite and recommend within the evidence.

topics.title: Research and its quality
topics.core: Research is systematic inquiry using evidence to answer questions or develop knowledge.
topics.explanation: Good research is systematic, rigorous, empirical, critical, and sufficiently transparent to be checked. Appropriate control and valid measurement strengthen claims; perfect control is rarely possible in human settings.
topics.example: Record classroom participation using defined rules, then analyse the pattern rather than relying on a teacher's impression.
topics.confusion: Following steps neatly does not make a weak measurement valid.

questions.prompt: Explain research and its quality briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Research is systematic inquiry using evidence to answer questions or develop knowledge.
questions.answer: Research is systematic inquiry using evidence to answer questions or develop knowledge. Good research is systematic, rigorous, empirical, critical, and sufficiently transparent to be checked.
keyPoints: Research is systematic inquiry using evidence to answer questions or develop knowledge.

questions.prompt: A teacher says students seem more fluent. What would turn that impression into research?
questions.shortAnswer: Define fluency, formulate a focused question, collect suitable performance evidence, analyse it systematically and acknowledge alternative explanations.
questions.answer: Define fluency, formulate a focused question, collect suitable performance evidence, analyse it systematically and acknowledge alternative explanations.
keyPoints: Define fluency, formulate a focused question, collect suitable performance evidence, analyse it systematically and acknowledge alternative explanations.

topics.title: Qualitative research
topics.core: Qualitative research interprets meanings, experiences and practices in context.
topics.explanation: It commonly works with interviews, observations and texts. The researcher explains how evidence supports an interpretation, including cases that challenge it.
topics.example: Interview quiet learners to understand how they experience speaking in class.
topics.confusion: Qualitative does not mean unsystematic or simply non-numerical description.

questions.prompt: What is qualitative research?
questions.shortAnswer: Qualitative research interprets meanings, experiences and practices in context.
questions.answer: Qualitative research interprets meanings, experiences and practices in context. It commonly works with interviews, observations and texts.
keyPoints: Qualitative research interprets meanings, experiences and practices in context.

questions.prompt: Why might interviews help explain classroom silence better than a score alone?
questions.shortAnswer: Interviews can reveal meanings such as fear of peer judgment that a score does not capture.
questions.answer: Interviews can reveal meanings such as fear of peer judgment that a score does not capture. Accounts still need contextual analysis and do not directly prove actual behaviour.
keyPoints: Interviews can reveal meanings such as fear of peer judgment that a score does not capture.
Accounts still need contextual analysis and do not directly prove actual behaviour.

topics.title: Quantitative research
topics.core: Quantitative research measures variables and analyses numerical patterns, differences or relationships.
topics.explanation: Specify what is measured, how scores are produced, and what comparison answers the question. Numerical precision does not compensate for a poor construct measure.
topics.example: Compare fluency scores before and after a teaching intervention.
topics.confusion: A quantitative study need not be an experiment.

questions.prompt: What is quantitative research?
questions.shortAnswer: Quantitative research measures variables and analyses numerical patterns, differences or relationships.
questions.answer: Quantitative research measures variables and analyses numerical patterns, differences or relationships. Specify what is measured, how scores are produced, and what comparison answers the question.
keyPoints: Quantitative research measures variables and analyses numerical patterns, differences or relationships.

questions.prompt: Is counting the number of English words in student essays quantitative research?
questions.shortAnswer: It can be quantitative if the counts answer a clear question through systematic sampling and analysis.
questions.answer: It can be quantitative if the counts answer a clear question through systematic sampling and analysis. Counting alone is insufficient without a reasoned design and interpretation.
keyPoints: It can be quantitative if the counts answer a clear question through systematic sampling and analysis.
Counting alone is insufficient without a reasoned design and interpretation.

topics.title: Mixed methods
topics.core: Mixed methods integrates qualitative and quantitative evidence in one investigation.
topics.explanation: The strands may be sequential, concurrent, embedded or multiphase. Explain where they connect: design, sampling, analysis or interpretation.
topics.example: Compare speaking scores, then interview learners to explain contrasting gains.
topics.confusion: A questionnaire with an open comment box is not automatically a mixed-methods study.

questions.prompt: Explain mixed methods briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Mixed methods integrates qualitative and quantitative evidence in one investigation.
questions.answer: Mixed methods integrates qualitative and quantitative evidence in one investigation. The strands may be sequential, concurrent, embedded or multiphase.
keyPoints: Mixed methods integrates qualitative and quantitative evidence in one investigation.

questions.prompt: You collect test scores and interviews but discuss them separately. What is missing?
questions.shortAnswer: A clear integration of the two strands.
questions.answer: A clear integration of the two strands. Explain how interview findings help interpret, challenge or extend the numerical results.
keyPoints: A clear integration of the two strands.
Explain how interview findings help interpret, challenge or extend the numerical results.

topics.title: Research classifications
topics.core: A study can receive different labels according to its purpose, objective, evidence, timing and design.
topics.explanation: Basic research primarily develops knowledge; applied research addresses a practical problem. Exploratory, descriptive, correlational and explanatory labels concern the aim. These classifications can overlap.
topics.example: A classroom experiment may be applied, quantitative, explanatory and longitudinal.
topics.confusion: Basic research can have practical consequences; applied research can develop theory.

questions.prompt: Explain research classifications briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A study can receive different labels according to its purpose, objective, evidence, timing and design.
questions.answer: A study can receive different labels according to its purpose, objective, evidence, timing and design. Basic research primarily develops knowledge; applied research addresses a practical problem.
keyPoints: A study can receive different labels according to its purpose, objective, evidence, timing and design.

questions.prompt: Can a study be both applied and qualitative?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. Applied describes its practical purpose, while qualitative describes its approach to evidence and interpretation. They classify different aspects of the study.
keyPoints: Yes.
Applied describes its practical purpose, while qualitative describes its approach to evidence and interpretation.
They classify different aspects of the study.

topics.title: Induction and deduction
topics.core: Induction develops explanations from observations; deduction tests implications of existing explanations.
topics.explanation: Inductive reasoning moves from cases to patterns. Deductive reasoning moves from theory through a prediction to evidence. Studies may alternate between them.
topics.example: Develop a model of speaking anxiety from interviews, then test its predictions in another group.
topics.confusion: A supported prediction does not prove a theory universally.

questions.prompt: Explain induction and deduction briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Induction develops explanations from observations; deduction tests implications of existing explanations.
questions.answer: Induction develops explanations from observations; deduction tests implications of existing explanations. Inductive reasoning moves from cases to patterns.
keyPoints: Induction develops explanations from observations; deduction tests implications of existing explanations.

questions.prompt: You start with a theory and predict higher fluency after practice. Which reasoning is this?
questions.shortAnswer: Deductive reasoning: the prediction follows from an existing explanation and is checked against data.
questions.answer: Deductive reasoning: the prediction follows from an existing explanation and is checked against data. Unexpected results may prompt inductive revision.
keyPoints: Deductive reasoning: the prediction follows from an existing explanation and is checked against data.
Unexpected results may prompt inductive revision.

topics.title: Longitudinal and cross-sectional designs
topics.core: Longitudinal designs collect evidence over time; cross-sectional designs examine a population or groups at one time.
topics.explanation: Panel designs repeatedly study the same individuals. Trend designs can use different samples from the same population; cohort designs focus on a group sharing a starting feature. Timing is separate from whether a study is experimental.
topics.example: Follow the same learners across semesters to track vocabulary development, or compare year groups at one time for a cross-sectional snapshot.
topics.confusion: A difference between year groups does not directly measure change within the same individuals.

questions.prompt: Explain longitudinal and cross-sectional designs briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Longitudinal designs collect evidence over time; cross-sectional designs examine a population or groups at one time.
questions.answer: Longitudinal designs collect evidence over time; cross-sectional designs examine a population or groups at one time. Panel designs repeatedly study the same individuals.
keyPoints: Longitudinal designs collect evidence over time; cross-sectional designs examine a population or groups at one time.

questions.prompt: Why might a panel design help investigate language development?
questions.shortAnswer: Repeated observations of the same learners can show individual change over time.
questions.answer: Repeated observations of the same learners can show individual change over time. Comparable measures and attention to attrition are needed; observed change does not by itself establish its cause.
keyPoints: Repeated observations of the same learners can show individual change over time.
Comparable measures and attention to attrition are needed; observed change does not by itself establish its cause.

topics.title: Narrative inquiry
topics.core: Narrative inquiry studies how people organise and interpret experience through stories.
topics.explanation: Attend to sequence, turning points, identity and the setting in which a story is told. A story is a situated account rather than a transparent record of every event.
topics.example: Ask a teacher to narrate becoming an English teacher and analyse how key events shape professional identity.
topics.confusion: Narrative inquiry focuses on story construction, not merely extracting isolated themes.

questions.prompt: What is narrative inquiry?
questions.shortAnswer: Narrative inquiry studies how people organise and interpret experience through stories.
questions.answer: Narrative inquiry studies how people organise and interpret experience through stories. Attend to sequence, turning points, identity and the setting in which a story is told.
keyPoints: Narrative inquiry studies how people organise and interpret experience through stories.

questions.prompt: How would you investigate a learner's changing relationship with English through narrative inquiry?
questions.shortAnswer: Invite a learning-history account, examine turning points and identity positions, and relate the telling to its social context.
questions.answer: Invite a learning-history account, examine turning points and identity positions, and relate the telling to its social context. Preserve the sequence and the learner's meaning-making.
keyPoints: Invite a learning-history account, examine turning points and identity positions, and relate the telling to its social context.
Preserve the sequence and the learner's meaning-making.

topics.title: Case study
topics.core: A case study examines a bounded case in depth within its real context.
topics.explanation: A case may be a person, class, programme or institution. Define boundaries of place, time and activity and use suitable evidence such as interviews, observations and documents.
topics.example: Study one Grade 8 class's group work during one academic year.
topics.confusion: A case is a bounded unit; it is not automatically a representative sample.

questions.prompt: What is case study?
questions.shortAnswer: A case study examines a bounded case in depth within its real context.
questions.answer: A case study examines a bounded case in depth within its real context. A case may be a person, class, programme or institution.
keyPoints: A case study examines a bounded case in depth within its real context.

questions.prompt: Why is 'students in Bangladesh' too vague as a case-study boundary?
questions.shortAnswer: It does not identify a specific bounded case.
questions.answer: It does not identify a specific bounded case. Specify a class, institution, group or programme and define its time, place and activity boundaries.
keyPoints: It does not identify a specific bounded case.
Specify a class, institution, group or programme and define its time, place and activity boundaries.

topics.title: Case-study types
topics.core: Intrinsic studies examine a case for its own interest; instrumental studies use it to understand a wider issue.
topics.explanation: Collective studies compare cases. Embedded studies examine subunits; holistic studies treat the case as one unit. Longitudinal refers to time and can combine with the other labels.
topics.example: One school may be an instrumental case with three embedded classroom units.
topics.confusion: These labels are based on different dimensions and are not mutually exclusive.

questions.prompt: Explain case-study types briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Intrinsic studies examine a case for its own interest; instrumental studies use it to understand a wider issue.
questions.answer: Intrinsic studies examine a case for its own interest; instrumental studies use it to understand a wider issue. Collective studies compare cases.
keyPoints: Intrinsic studies examine a case for its own interest; instrumental studies use it to understand a wider issue.

questions.prompt: Can a case study be instrumental, embedded and longitudinal at once?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. It can illuminate a broader issue, examine classroom subunits and follow the school over time. Each label describes a different feature.
keyPoints: Yes.
It can illuminate a broader issue, examine classroom subunits and follow the school over time.
Each label describes a different feature.

topics.title: Action research
topics.core: Action research is a practitioner's systematic cycle of investigating and improving local practice.
topics.explanation: A typical cycle is plan, act, observe and reflect, followed by revision. The evidence may be qualitative, quantitative or mixed. Improvement claims need evidence rather than enthusiasm alone.
topics.example: A teacher changes feedback routines, observes participation, reflects and adjusts the next lesson cycle.
topics.confusion: Trying a new activity without systematic investigation is not enough.

questions.prompt: What is action research?
questions.shortAnswer: Action research is a practitioner's systematic cycle of investigating and improving local practice.
questions.answer: Action research is a practitioner's systematic cycle of investigating and improving local practice. A typical cycle is plan, act, observe and reflect, followed by revision.
keyPoints: Action research is a practitioner's systematic cycle of investigating and improving local practice.

questions.prompt: A teacher introduces peer feedback. What makes this action research?
questions.shortAnswer: The teacher identifies a problem, plans a change, gathers evidence during implementation, reflects on the outcome and uses it to plan another cycle.
questions.answer: The teacher identifies a problem, plans a change, gathers evidence during implementation, reflects on the outcome and uses it to plan another cycle.
keyPoints: The teacher identifies a problem, plans a change, gathers evidence during implementation, reflects on the outcome and uses it to plan another cycle.

topics.title: Grounded theory
topics.core: Grounded theory develops an explanatory theory or model through systematic analysis of data.
topics.explanation: Coding and comparison support progressively developed categories and their relationships. Theory development is central; a list of themes alone does not establish grounded theory.
topics.example: Develop a model of how new teachers adapt to unfamiliar classroom demands.
topics.confusion: Thematic analysis and grounded theory can both code data, but their aims differ.

questions.prompt: What is grounded theory?
questions.shortAnswer: Grounded theory develops an explanatory theory or model through systematic analysis of data.
questions.answer: Grounded theory develops an explanatory theory or model through systematic analysis of data. Coding and comparison support progressively developed categories and their relationships.
keyPoints: Grounded theory develops an explanatory theory or model through systematic analysis of data.

questions.prompt: Why is an interview study with five themes not necessarily grounded theory?
questions.shortAnswer: Themes can describe patterns without producing an explanatory model.
questions.answer: Themes can describe patterns without producing an explanatory model. Grounded theory requires a coherent account of processes and relationships developed through systematic comparative analysis.
keyPoints: Themes can describe patterns without producing an explanatory model.
Grounded theory requires a coherent account of processes and relationships developed through systematic comparative analysis.

topics.title: Survey research
topics.core: Survey research systematically collects information about a population or sample's characteristics, behaviour or views.
topics.explanation: Questionnaires and interviews are possible instruments. Plan the sample, pilot questions, collect and prepare responses, analyse and report the findings and limits.
topics.example: Survey learners' reported weekly English practice and attitudes.
topics.confusion: A survey is a design; a questionnaire is a tool within it.

questions.prompt: What is survey research?
questions.shortAnswer: Survey research systematically collects information about a population or sample's characteristics, behaviour or views.
questions.answer: Survey research systematically collects information about a population or sample's characteristics, behaviour or views. Questionnaires and interviews are possible instruments.
keyPoints: Survey research systematically collects information about a population or sample's characteristics, behaviour or views.

questions.prompt: Does a survey showing students like an app prove the app improves learning?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. It measures reported preference or perception. Evidence of learning improvement requires an appropriate performance measure and design.
keyPoints: No.
It measures reported preference or perception.
Evidence of learning improvement requires an appropriate performance measure and design.

topics.title: Experimental and quasi-experimental research
topics.core: An experiment manipulates an independent variable to examine an outcome; a true experiment uses random assignment.
topics.explanation: A quasi-experiment studies an intervention without random allocation, often in intact classes. Comparison groups and baseline measures help address alternative explanations.
topics.example: Randomly assign learners to two feedback conditions and compare writing outcomes.
topics.confusion: Random sampling selects participants; random assignment allocates conditions.

questions.prompt: Explain experimental and quasi-experimental research briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: An experiment manipulates an independent variable to examine an outcome; a true experiment uses random assignment.
questions.answer: An experiment manipulates an independent variable to examine an outcome; a true experiment uses random assignment. A quasi-experiment studies an intervention without random allocation, often in intact classes.
keyPoints: An experiment manipulates an independent variable to examine an outcome; a true experiment uses random assignment.

questions.prompt: Two existing classes receive different teaching methods. Is this a true experiment?
questions.shortAnswer: Usually it is quasi-experimental because learners were not randomly assigned.
questions.answer: Usually it is quasi-experimental because learners were not randomly assigned. Initial class differences and teacher differences may influence the outcomes.
keyPoints: Usually it is quasi-experimental because learners were not randomly assigned.
Initial class differences and teacher differences may influence the outcomes.

topics.title: Experimental designs
topics.core: A pretest-posttest control-group design compares groups before and after an intervention.
topics.explanation: Posttest-only designs avoid pretest sensitisation but lack direct individual gains. Repeated measures reuse participants; factorial designs examine multiple factors; Solomon designs examine pretest effects.
topics.example: Measure fluency in both teaching groups before and after four weeks.
topics.confusion: Improvement in one group alone is not evidence that its method caused the change.

questions.prompt: Explain experimental designs briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A pretest-posttest control-group design compares groups before and after an intervention.
questions.answer: A pretest-posttest control-group design compares groups before and after an intervention. Posttest-only designs avoid pretest sensitisation but lack direct individual gains.
keyPoints: A pretest-posttest control-group design compares groups before and after an intervention.

questions.prompt: Why include a comparison group when test scores improve after teaching?
questions.shortAnswer: It helps separate the intervention effect from maturation, test practice and other changes.
questions.answer: It helps separate the intervention effect from maturation, test practice and other changes. Compare groups with suitable baseline and design controls.
keyPoints: It helps separate the intervention effect from maturation, test practice and other changes.
Compare groups with suitable baseline and design controls.

topics.title: Corpus research
topics.core: Corpus research studies language patterns in systematically assembled collections of texts or speech.
topics.explanation: Searchable corpora support analyses of frequency, collocation and variation. Corpus selection must fit the research question; numerical patterns still require contextual interpretation.
topics.example: Compare how often academic and conversational corpora use a target phrase.
topics.confusion: A large collection is not automatically representative of all language use.

questions.prompt: What is corpus research?
questions.shortAnswer: Corpus research studies language patterns in systematically assembled collections of texts or speech.
questions.answer: Corpus research studies language patterns in systematically assembled collections of texts or speech. Searchable corpora support analyses of frequency, collocation and variation.
keyPoints: Corpus research studies language patterns in systematically assembled collections of texts or speech.

questions.prompt: Why should raw word counts from differently sized corpora be normalised?
questions.shortAnswer: A larger corpus naturally contains more tokens.
questions.answer: A larger corpus naturally contains more tokens. Rates per a common number of words permit a fairer frequency comparison, alongside attention to sampling and context.
keyPoints: A larger corpus naturally contains more tokens.
Rates per a common number of words permit a fairer frequency comparison, alongside attention to sampling and context.

topics.title: Digital discourse research
topics.core: Digital discourse research investigates communication mediated by digital platforms.
topics.explanation: The research design considers platform features, participants, multimodal communication, data boundaries and ethical use. The same text can function differently across platforms and audiences.
topics.example: Analyse how replies, emojis and quoted posts organise disagreement in a class discussion forum.
topics.confusion: An online questionnaire is a digital collection tool, not automatically a study of digital discourse.

questions.prompt: What is digital discourse research?
questions.shortAnswer: Digital discourse research investigates communication mediated by digital platforms.
questions.answer: Digital discourse research investigates communication mediated by digital platforms. The research design considers platform features, participants, multimodal communication, data boundaries and ethical use.
keyPoints: Digital discourse research investigates communication mediated by digital platforms.

questions.prompt: Why must a study of online disagreement consider platform design?
questions.shortAnswer: Features such as reply threading, visibility and character limits shape how messages are produced and interpreted.
questions.answer: Features such as reply threading, visibility and character limits shape how messages are produced and interpreted. Analysis should connect linguistic choices with these technical and social conditions.
keyPoints: Features such as reply threading, visibility and character limits shape how messages are produced and interpreted.
Analysis should connect linguistic choices with these technical and social conditions.

topics.title: Psycholinguistic methods
topics.core: Psycholinguistic methods investigate language processing through controlled tasks and behavioural or physiological measures.
topics.explanation: Reaction times, accuracy and eye movements provide evidence about processing under specified task conditions. They require an explicit inference linking an observable measure to a mental process.
topics.example: Compare reading times at an ambiguous phrase and a matched unambiguous phrase.
topics.confusion: A slow response is evidence requiring interpretation, not a direct reading of a thought.

questions.prompt: Explain psycholinguistic methods briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Psycholinguistic methods investigate language processing through controlled tasks and behavioural or physiological measures.
questions.answer: Psycholinguistic methods investigate language processing through controlled tasks and behavioural or physiological measures. Reaction times, accuracy and eye movements provide evidence about processing under specified task conditions.
keyPoints: Psycholinguistic methods investigate language processing through controlled tasks and behavioural or physiological measures.

questions.prompt: Why record both accuracy and response time in a lexical-decision task?
questions.shortAnswer: Response time can indicate processing difficulty, but faster responses may be less accurate.
questions.answer: Response time can indicate processing difficulty, but faster responses may be less accurate. Considering both helps evaluate task performance and a possible speed–accuracy trade-off.
keyPoints: Response time can indicate processing difficulty, but faster responses may be less accurate.
Considering both helps evaluate task performance and a possible speed–accuracy trade-off.

topics.title: Critical research
topics.core: Critical research explicitly examines power, inequality and the assumptions shaping knowledge or practice.
topics.explanation: It asks whose interests are served and whose experiences are excluded. In language research, claims about ideology should be grounded in evidence and context, with attention to the researcher's own position.
topics.example: Examine whose English varieties are treated as legitimate in classroom materials.
topics.confusion: Critical does not simply mean finding faults or announcing a political conclusion.

questions.prompt: What is critical research?
questions.shortAnswer: Critical research explicitly examines power, inequality and the assumptions shaping knowledge or practice.
questions.answer: Critical research explicitly examines power, inequality and the assumptions shaping knowledge or practice. It asks whose interests are served and whose experiences are excluded.
keyPoints: Critical research explicitly examines power, inequality and the assumptions shaping knowledge or practice.

questions.prompt: How would a critical study examine an English-only classroom policy?
questions.shortAnswer: Investigate whose opportunities and identities the policy supports or restricts, analyse its language and implementation, and consider participants' experiences and institutional power.
questions.answer: Investigate whose opportunities and identities the policy supports or restricts, analyse its language and implementation, and consider participants' experiences and institutional power.
keyPoints: Investigate whose opportunities and identities the policy supports or restricts, analyse its language and implementation, and consider participants' experiences and institutional power.

topics.title: Interdisciplinary research
topics.core: Interdisciplinary research combines concepts or methods from different fields to address a shared question.
topics.explanation: The contribution comes from integration: perspectives should jointly explain the problem. Language learning can involve linguistic, psychological, social and educational processes.
topics.example: Study speaking anxiety using psycholinguistic processing measures and sociolinguistic analysis of classroom identity.
topics.confusion: Placing unrelated findings side by side is not strong integration.

questions.prompt: What is interdisciplinary research?
questions.shortAnswer: Interdisciplinary research combines concepts or methods from different fields to address a shared question.
questions.answer: Interdisciplinary research combines concepts or methods from different fields to address a shared question. The contribution comes from integration: perspectives should jointly explain the problem.
keyPoints: Interdisciplinary research combines concepts or methods from different fields to address a shared question.

questions.prompt: How could linguistics and psychology jointly study oral participation?
questions.shortAnswer: Linguistic analysis can examine interaction patterns while psychological measures explore anxiety or processing demands.
questions.answer: Linguistic analysis can examine interaction patterns while psychological measures explore anxiety or processing demands. Integrate the evidence to explain when and why learners participate.
keyPoints: Linguistic analysis can examine interaction patterns while psychological measures explore anxiety or processing demands.
Integrate the evidence to explain when and why learners participate.

topics.title: Discourse analysis and CDA
topics.core: Discourse analysis studies language in use; critical discourse analysis explicitly investigates power and ideology in discourse.
topics.explanation: Both consider context and what communication does. CDA examines how inequality is sustained or challenged through representation, interaction and institutions.
topics.example: Analyse who receives speaking turns; a CDA study additionally asks how those patterns reproduce authority or exclusion.
topics.confusion: Ordinary discourse analysis is not restricted to sentence grammar.

questions.prompt: Explain discourse analysis and cda briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Discourse analysis studies language in use; critical discourse analysis explicitly investigates power and ideology in discourse.
questions.answer: Discourse analysis studies language in use; critical discourse analysis explicitly investigates power and ideology in discourse. Both consider context and what communication does.
keyPoints: Discourse analysis studies language in use; critical discourse analysis explicitly investigates power and ideology in discourse.

questions.prompt: How could two researchers analyse the same textbook differently using DA and CDA?
questions.shortAnswer: One may examine how explanations and tasks construct meanings.
questions.answer: One may examine how explanations and tasks construct meanings. A critical analysis would explicitly investigate whose identities and interests are privileged or marginalised, linking textual evidence to social power.
keyPoints: One may examine how explanations and tasks construct meanings.
A critical analysis would explicitly investigate whose identities and interests are privileged or marginalised, linking textual evidence to social power.

topics.title: Ethnography and reflexivity
topics.core: Ethnography investigates a group's shared practices and meanings through sustained contextual engagement.
topics.explanation: Participant observation, field notes, interviews and artefacts help connect participants' emic meanings with analytical perspectives. Reflexivity examines the researcher's influence and assumptions.
topics.example: Follow a multilingual class over time to understand when code-switching signals solidarity.
topics.confusion: One classroom visit is not a full ethnography.

questions.prompt: Explain ethnography and reflexivity briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Ethnography investigates a group's shared practices and meanings through sustained contextual engagement.
questions.answer: Ethnography investigates a group's shared practices and meanings through sustained contextual engagement. Participant observation, field notes, interviews and artefacts help connect participants' emic meanings with analytical perspectives.
keyPoints: Ethnography investigates a group's shared practices and meanings through sustained contextual engagement.

questions.prompt: What makes a description of code-switching 'thick'?
questions.shortAnswer: It explains the interaction's setting, participants, timing and social meaning, rather than simply recording that a language switch occurred.
questions.answer: It explains the interaction's setting, participants, timing and social meaning, rather than simply recording that a language switch occurred.
keyPoints: It explains the interaction's setting, participants, timing and social meaning, rather than simply recording that a language switch occurred.

topics.title: Research problem and scope
topics.core: A research problem identifies a specific uncertainty or difficulty requiring investigation.
topics.explanation: A problem statement sets the context, explains what is not adequately understood and defines boundaries. The four Ps—people, problems, programmes and phenomena—can help locate a manageable focus.
topics.example: Narrow 'English speaking' to peer judgment and participation among first-year students in one department.
topics.confusion: A broad topic or interesting title is not yet a research problem.

questions.prompt: Explain research problem and scope briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A research problem identifies a specific uncertainty or difficulty requiring investigation.
questions.answer: A research problem identifies a specific uncertainty or difficulty requiring investigation. A problem statement sets the context, explains what is not adequately understood and defines boundaries.
keyPoints: A research problem identifies a specific uncertainty or difficulty requiring investigation.

questions.prompt: How would you narrow 'technology and English learning' into a researchable problem?
questions.shortAnswer: Select a population, setting, activity and uncertainty—for example, how first-year learners use mobile dictionaries during reading tasks—and check that evidence is accessible.
questions.answer: Select a population, setting, activity and uncertainty—for example, how first-year learners use mobile dictionaries during reading tasks—and check that evidence is accessible.
keyPoints: Select a population, setting, activity and uncertainty—for example, how first-year learners use mobile dictionaries during reading tasks—and check that evidence is accessible.

topics.title: Research objectives and justification
topics.core: Objectives state what the study will achieve; justification explains why that achievement matters.
topics.explanation: Use clear action verbs such as describe, examine or compare. Link each objective to a research question and explain its theoretical, practical or stakeholder relevance.
topics.example: Objective: compare fluency gains. Justification: clarify whether the activity warrants classroom time.
topics.confusion: Expected contribution is not a promise of positive results.

questions.prompt: Explain research objectives and justification briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Objectives state what the study will achieve; justification explains why that achievement matters.
questions.answer: Objectives state what the study will achieve; justification explains why that achievement matters. Use clear action verbs such as describe, examine or compare.
keyPoints: Objectives state what the study will achieve; justification explains why that achievement matters.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with the objective 'to prove role-play is effective'?
questions.shortAnswer: It prejudges the outcome.
questions.answer: It prejudges the outcome. Use an open, measurable objective such as comparing fluency outcomes under role-play and usual instruction.
keyPoints: It prejudges the outcome.
Use an open, measurable objective such as comparing fluency outcomes under role-play and usual instruction.

topics.title: Research questions and hypotheses
topics.core: A research question asks what will be investigated; a hypothesis predicts a testable relationship or outcome.
topics.explanation: Questions should be focused, researchable and aligned with obtainable evidence. A null hypothesis commonly specifies no population difference; an alternative specifies a difference. Exploratory studies may use questions without formal hypotheses.
topics.example: Ask whether feedback type affects revision quality; predict greater improvement with one type.
topics.confusion: A hypothesis is provisional, not an established fact.

questions.prompt: Explain research questions and hypotheses briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A research question asks what will be investigated; a hypothesis predicts a testable relationship or outcome.
questions.answer: A research question asks what will be investigated; a hypothesis predicts a testable relationship or outcome. Questions should be focused, researchable and aligned with obtainable evidence.
keyPoints: A research question asks what will be investigated; a hypothesis predicts a testable relationship or outcome.

questions.prompt: Does every qualitative study need a formal hypothesis?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. Exploratory qualitative research often uses open research questions to understand meanings and processes without a predetermined statistical prediction.
keyPoints: No.
Exploratory qualitative research often uses open research questions to understand meanings and processes without a predetermined statistical prediction.

topics.title: Operational definitions and variables
topics.core: An operational definition states how a concept will be observed or measured in a particular study.
topics.explanation: Distinguish the independent variable, outcome variable and possible confound. The operational measure must fit the construct and its limits must be acknowledged.
topics.example: Define a fluency measure as words per minute during a comparable two-minute speaking task.
topics.confusion: Words per minute measures one aspect of fluency, not all speaking ability.

questions.prompt: Explain operational definitions and variables briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: An operational definition states how a concept will be observed or measured in a particular study.
questions.answer: An operational definition states how a concept will be observed or measured in a particular study. Distinguish the independent variable, outcome variable and possible confound.
keyPoints: An operational definition states how a concept will be observed or measured in a particular study.

questions.prompt: Why is 'students improved their English' an inadequate operational definition?
questions.shortAnswer: It does not specify which ability, measurement task, scoring rule or comparison establishes improvement.
questions.answer: It does not specify which ability, measurement task, scoring rule or comparison establishes improvement. Define an observable outcome linked to the research question.
keyPoints: It does not specify which ability, measurement task, scoring rule or comparison establishes improvement.
Define an observable outcome linked to the research question.

topics.title: Limitations and confounds
topics.core: Limitations are constraints on the strength, scope or interpretation of a study's conclusions.
topics.explanation: Discuss sampling bias, measurement limits, confounding and contextual boundaries. A confound varies with the proposed cause and can influence the outcome, creating a competing explanation.
topics.example: Only the experimental class has a highly experienced teacher.
topics.confusion: A large sample cannot repair a biased selection method.

questions.prompt: Explain limitations and confounds briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Limitations are constraints on the strength, scope or interpretation of a study's conclusions.
questions.answer: Limitations are constraints on the strength, scope or interpretation of a study's conclusions. Discuss sampling bias, measurement limits, confounding and contextual boundaries.
keyPoints: Limitations are constraints on the strength, scope or interpretation of a study's conclusions.

questions.prompt: The new method's group has the best teacher. What threatens the conclusion?
questions.shortAnswer: Teacher experience is confounded with method.
questions.answer: Teacher experience is confounded with method. Differences could reflect teaching expertise rather than the method, so the design or conclusion must address that alternative.
keyPoints: Teacher experience is confounded with method.
Differences could reflect teaching expertise rather than the method, so the design or conclusion must address that alternative.

topics.title: Literature review and synthesis
topics.core: A literature review critically synthesises relevant research to establish what is known, debated and missing.
topics.explanation: Search, evaluate, compare themes and methods, organise the argument, then connect the review to the study. Thematic, chronological, methodological and theoretical structures are possible.
topics.example: Compare surveys and observations of anxiety instead of listing one author after another.
topics.confusion: An annotated bibliography describes individual sources; a review connects them.
syllabusTerms: Literature review: what, why and how

questions.prompt: Explain literature review and synthesis briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A literature review critically synthesises relevant research to establish what is known, debated and missing.
questions.answer: A literature review critically synthesises relevant research to establish what is known, debated and missing. Search, evaluate, compare themes and methods, organise the argument, then connect the review to the study.
keyPoints: A literature review critically synthesises relevant research to establish what is known, debated and missing.

questions.prompt: How can a literature review justify a new study without claiming that nobody studied the topic?
questions.shortAnswer: Identify a specific unresolved issue supported by the reviewed evidence, such as limited observation of a particular population or disagreement between findings.
questions.answer: Identify a specific unresolved issue supported by the reviewed evidence, such as limited observation of a particular population or disagreement between findings.
keyPoints: Identify a specific unresolved issue supported by the reviewed evidence, such as limited observation of a particular population or disagreement between findings.

topics.title: Research gaps
topics.core: A research gap is an important absence, weakness or unresolved issue in existing knowledge.
topics.explanation: The guide distinguishes evidence, knowledge, methodological, population, theoretical, empirical and practical-knowledge gaps. Categories can overlap, so explain the specific missing element.
topics.example: Several studies use self-report only; observation could address a methodological gap.
topics.confusion: A topic being new to you does not make it a research gap.
syllabusTerms: Literature review: what, why and how

questions.prompt: Explain research gaps briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A research gap is an important absence, weakness or unresolved issue in existing knowledge.
questions.answer: A research gap is an important absence, weakness or unresolved issue in existing knowledge. The guide distinguishes evidence, knowledge, methodological, population, theoretical, empirical and practical-knowledge gaps.
keyPoints: A research gap is an important absence, weakness or unresolved issue in existing knowledge.

questions.prompt: How does a population gap differ from a methodological gap?
questions.shortAnswer: A population gap concerns an underrepresented group.
questions.answer: A population gap concerns an underrepresented group. A methodological gap concerns limitations in how evidence was obtained or analysed; one study may address both.
keyPoints: A population gap concerns an underrepresented group.
A methodological gap concerns limitations in how evidence was obtained or analysed; one study may address both.

topics.title: Population, sample and sampling
topics.core: A population is the defined group of interest; a sample is the subset actually investigated.
topics.explanation: Sampling specifies how units enter the study. Define the target population, accessible population, selection procedure and reasons for sample size.
topics.example: Select 40 learners from a department of 400.
topics.confusion: A sample is not automatically representative because it is large.

questions.prompt: Explain population, sample and sampling briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A population is the defined group of interest; a sample is the subset actually investigated.
questions.answer: A population is the defined group of interest; a sample is the subset actually investigated. Sampling specifies how units enter the study.
keyPoints: A population is the defined group of interest; a sample is the subset actually investigated.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between random selection and random assignment?
questions.shortAnswer: Selection chooses who enters the sample; assignment places sampled participants into study conditions.
questions.answer: Selection chooses who enters the sample; assignment places sampled participants into study conditions. The former supports representativeness, while the latter helps reduce confounding.
keyPoints: Selection chooses who enters the sample; assignment places sampled participants into study conditions.
The former supports representativeness, while the latter helps reduce confounding.

topics.title: Probability sampling
topics.core: Probability sampling gives each population member a known non-zero chance of selection.
topics.explanation: Simple random sampling selects individuals; systematic sampling uses a random start and interval; stratified sampling draws within subgroups; cluster sampling selects natural groups.
topics.example: Randomly select learners within each academic year for a stratified sample.
topics.confusion: Probability sampling does not always give equal selection chances.

questions.prompt: What is probability sampling?
questions.shortAnswer: Probability sampling gives each population member a known non-zero chance of selection.
questions.answer: Probability sampling gives each population member a known non-zero chance of selection. Simple random sampling selects individuals; systematic sampling uses a random start and interval; stratified sampling draws within subgroups; cluster sampling selects natural groups..
keyPoints: Probability sampling gives each population member a known non-zero chance of selection.

questions.prompt: How do stratified and cluster sampling differ?
questions.shortAnswer: Stratified sampling draws from each relevant subgroup.
questions.answer: Stratified sampling draws from each relevant subgroup. Cluster sampling selects some natural groups, then studies all or sampled members within those groups.
keyPoints: Stratified sampling draws from each relevant subgroup.
Cluster sampling selects some natural groups, then studies all or sampled members within those groups.

topics.title: Non-probability sampling
topics.core: Non-probability sampling selects cases without known random selection probabilities.
topics.explanation: Convenience selects accessible participants; purposive selects relevant experience; snowball uses referrals; quota fills subgroup targets without random selection; maximum variation seeks diverse cases.
topics.example: Recruit teachers with experience of multilingual classrooms for in-depth interviews.
topics.confusion: Purposive selection can serve a qualitative goal without supporting statistical representativeness.

questions.prompt: What is non-probability sampling?
questions.shortAnswer: Non-probability sampling selects cases without known random selection probabilities.
questions.answer: Non-probability sampling selects cases without known random selection probabilities. Convenience selects accessible participants; purposive selects relevant experience; snowball uses referrals; quota fills subgroup targets without random selection; maximum variation seeks diverse cases..
keyPoints: Non-probability sampling selects cases without known random selection probabilities.

questions.prompt: Why might purposive sampling fit an interview study better than convenience sampling?
questions.shortAnswer: The research may require participants with particular experiences.
questions.answer: The research may require participants with particular experiences. Purposeful selection aligns the evidence with that focus rather than relying only on whoever is easiest to reach.
keyPoints: The research may require participants with particular experiences.
Purposeful selection aligns the evidence with that focus rather than relying only on whoever is easiest to reach.

topics.title: Sample size and saturation
topics.core: Sample size should fit the research question, variation, analytical needs and available resources.
topics.explanation: Quantitative studies consider precision and power; qualitative studies consider information richness and adequacy. Saturation refers to diminishing relevant new information, not a universal interview count.
topics.example: A diverse population may require broader sampling than one narrow experiential group.
topics.confusion: A fixed number such as 20 interviews does not guarantee saturation.

questions.prompt: Explain sample size and saturation briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Sample size should fit the research question, variation, analytical needs and available resources.
questions.answer: Sample size should fit the research question, variation, analytical needs and available resources. Quantitative studies consider precision and power; qualitative studies consider information richness and adequacy.
keyPoints: Sample size should fit the research question, variation, analytical needs and available resources.

questions.prompt: Why is 'I interviewed 20 people, therefore saturation occurred' weak reasoning?
questions.shortAnswer: The adequacy of the data depends on diversity, depth, scope and analysis.
questions.answer: The adequacy of the data depends on diversity, depth, scope and analysis. Explain what additional interviews contributed and how the relevant categories became sufficiently developed.
keyPoints: The adequacy of the data depends on diversity, depth, scope and analysis.
Explain what additional interviews contributed and how the relevant categories became sufficiently developed.

topics.title: Questionnaires and instrumentation
topics.core: Instrumentation concerns the tools and procedures used to gather or measure evidence.
topics.explanation: A questionnaire can include closed, open or mixed items. Use neutral, clear wording, one issue per item, defined timeframes and a pilot. Match the response format to the evidence needed.
topics.example: Separate 'The app is easy and improves pronunciation' into two questions.
topics.confusion: A self-reported confidence scale is not a direct test of speaking skill.

questions.prompt: Explain questionnaires and instrumentation briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Instrumentation concerns the tools and procedures used to gather or measure evidence.
questions.answer: Instrumentation concerns the tools and procedures used to gather or measure evidence. A questionnaire can include closed, open or mixed items.
keyPoints: Instrumentation concerns the tools and procedures used to gather or measure evidence.

questions.prompt: Why is 'How helpful is this excellent app?' a poor questionnaire item?
questions.shortAnswer: It leads the respondent through positive wording.
questions.answer: It leads the respondent through positive wording. A neutral version asks how helpful, if at all, the app was and allows negative or uncertain responses.
keyPoints: It leads the respondent through positive wording.
A neutral version asks how helpful, if at all, the app was and allows negative or uncertain responses.

topics.title: Validity and reliability
topics.core: Validity concerns the appropriateness of an interpretation; reliability concerns measurement consistency.
topics.explanation: Use measures that fit the construct and procedures that minimise avoidable inconsistency. Training raters and piloting instruments can reveal weaknesses.
topics.example: Two raters consistently apply a speaking rubric, but a vocabulary-only test would inadequately represent fluency.
topics.confusion: Consistency alone does not establish validity.

questions.prompt: Explain validity and reliability briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Validity concerns the appropriateness of an interpretation; reliability concerns measurement consistency.
questions.answer: Validity concerns the appropriateness of an interpretation; reliability concerns measurement consistency. Use measures that fit the construct and procedures that minimise avoidable inconsistency.
keyPoints: Validity concerns the appropriateness of an interpretation; reliability concerns measurement consistency.

questions.prompt: Can an instrument be reliable but invalid for a purpose?
questions.shortAnswer: Yes.
questions.answer: Yes. It may consistently measure the wrong construct—for example, a stable vocabulary score used as if it fully measured spontaneous speaking fluency.
keyPoints: Yes.
It may consistently measure the wrong construct—for example, a stable vocabulary score used as if it fully measured spontaneous speaking fluency.

topics.title: Observation and interviews
topics.core: Observation records actions and interaction; interviews explore participants' accounts and interpretations.
topics.explanation: Specify observation categories, participation, disclosure and setting. Interviews may be structured, semi-structured or unstructured; flexible probes help clarify meaning.
topics.example: Observe participation and ask learners how they experienced the interaction.
topics.confusion: What people report doing can differ from what is observed.

questions.prompt: Explain observation and interviews briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Observation records actions and interaction; interviews explore participants' accounts and interpretations.
questions.answer: Observation records actions and interaction; interviews explore participants' accounts and interpretations. Specify observation categories, participation, disclosure and setting.
keyPoints: Observation records actions and interaction; interviews explore participants' accounts and interpretations.

questions.prompt: Why combine an interview with classroom observation?
questions.shortAnswer: Observation provides evidence of practice; interviews explain participants' meanings and experiences.
questions.answer: Observation provides evidence of practice; interviews explain participants' meanings and experiences. Their differences can identify questions that either source alone would miss.
keyPoints: Observation provides evidence of practice; interviews explain participants' meanings and experiences.
Their differences can identify questions that either source alone would miss.

topics.title: Triangulation
topics.core: Triangulation examines a phenomenon using multiple evidence sources or approaches.
topics.explanation: Comparing perspectives can strengthen an interpretation or expose contradictions. Disagreement should be investigated rather than hidden to produce apparent agreement.
topics.example: Compare learner interviews, class recordings and teacher notes about participation.
topics.confusion: Several methods do not automatically guarantee truth.

questions.prompt: What is triangulation?
questions.shortAnswer: Triangulation examines a phenomenon using multiple evidence sources or approaches.
questions.answer: Triangulation examines a phenomenon using multiple evidence sources or approaches. Comparing perspectives can strengthen an interpretation or expose contradictions.
keyPoints: Triangulation examines a phenomenon using multiple evidence sources or approaches.

questions.prompt: What should you do if interviews report high participation but observation shows little?
questions.shortAnswer: Examine the timeframe, definitions, observer effects and participants' interpretations.
questions.answer: Examine the timeframe, definitions, observer effects and participants' interpretations. The disagreement is evidence to explain, not a reason to discard an inconvenient source.
keyPoints: Examine the timeframe, definitions, observer effects and participants' interpretations.
The disagreement is evidence to explain, not a reason to discard an inconvenient source.

topics.title: Ethics and consent
topics.core: Research ethics requires informed, voluntary participation and appropriate protection of people and data.
topics.explanation: Explain the tasks, uses, risks, withdrawal conditions and privacy arrangements. Confidentiality protects identifiable information; anonymity means identities are not known or recorded in the relevant process.
topics.example: Explain recording use before an interview and avoid coercing students whose grades you control.
topics.confusion: Researchers cannot guarantee what fellow focus-group members will disclose later.

questions.prompt: Explain ethics and consent briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Research ethics requires informed, voluntary participation and appropriate protection of people and data.
questions.answer: Research ethics requires informed, voluntary participation and appropriate protection of people and data. Explain the tasks, uses, risks, withdrawal conditions and privacy arrangements.
keyPoints: Research ethics requires informed, voluntary participation and appropriate protection of people and data.

questions.prompt: Why is teacher-led research with the teacher's own students ethically sensitive?
questions.shortAnswer: The power relationship may make refusal feel unsafe.
questions.answer: The power relationship may make refusal feel unsafe. Participation and assessment should be separated, and students need a credible way to decline without disadvantage.
keyPoints: The power relationship may make refusal feel unsafe.
Participation and assessment should be separated, and students need a credible way to decline without disadvantage.

topics.title: Research transcription
topics.core: Transcription represents recorded speech in written form using conventions appropriate to the research question.
topics.explanation: Verbatim records retain relevant repetitions, pauses and false starts. Intelligent-verbatim and edited versions improve readability but may remove interactional evidence. Document decisions and check the record against the recording.
topics.example: Preserve a pause and self-correction when investigating repair, because their placement can explain how the exchange develops.
topics.confusion: A cleaned transcript is not a neutral copy: removing a feature can remove evidence.

questions.prompt: What is research transcription?
questions.shortAnswer: Transcription represents recorded speech in written form using conventions appropriate to the research question.
questions.answer: Transcription represents recorded speech in written form using conventions appropriate to the research question. Verbatim records retain relevant repetitions, pauses and false starts.
keyPoints: Transcription represents recorded speech in written form using conventions appropriate to the research question.

questions.prompt: Why might edited transcription be unsuitable for conversation analysis?
questions.shortAnswer: Editing can erase pauses, overlaps and repairs that show how turns and actions are organised.
questions.answer: Editing can erase pauses, overlaps and repairs that show how turns and actions are organised. Preserve the details needed by the analysis and state the transcription conventions.
keyPoints: Editing can erase pauses, overlaps and repairs that show how turns and actions are organised.
Preserve the details needed by the analysis and state the transcription conventions.

topics.title: Qualitative coding
topics.core: Coding labels meaningful data segments; analysis develops relationships and interpretations from those labels.
topics.explanation: Codes can form categories and themes. A theme should address a meaningful pattern relevant to the question, supported by extracts and checked against contrary cases.
topics.example: Code 'I stay quiet because classmates laugh' as fear of peer judgment.
topics.confusion: A frequent word or broad topic is not automatically an analytical theme.

questions.prompt: What is qualitative coding?
questions.shortAnswer: Coding labels meaningful data segments; analysis develops relationships and interpretations from those labels.
questions.answer: Coding labels meaningful data segments; analysis develops relationships and interpretations from those labels. Codes can form categories and themes.
keyPoints: Coding labels meaningful data segments; analysis develops relationships and interpretations from those labels.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between the code 'anxiety' and a developed theme?
questions.shortAnswer: A code labels a segment or idea.
questions.answer: A code labels a segment or idea. A theme articulates a broader pattern, such as peer judgment limiting participation, and explains its relevance across the evidence.
keyPoints: A code labels a segment or idea.
A theme articulates a broader pattern, such as peer judgment limiting participation, and explains its relevance across the evidence.

topics.title: Frequency and distributions
topics.core: Frequency counts occurrences; a distribution shows how observations are spread across values or categories.
topics.explanation: Tables and graphs reveal patterns, concentrations and variation. Percentages express counts relative to a total; check the denominator and missing data.
topics.example: 18 of 30 learners is 60 percent, provided all 30 supplied relevant responses.
topics.confusion: A numeric code for a category is not a measured quantity.

questions.prompt: Explain frequency and distributions briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Frequency counts occurrences; a distribution shows how observations are spread across values or categories.
questions.answer: Frequency counts occurrences; a distribution shows how observations are spread across values or categories. Tables and graphs reveal patterns, concentrations and variation.
keyPoints: Frequency counts occurrences; a distribution shows how observations are spread across values or categories.

questions.prompt: If 18 of 30 students use a dictionary daily, what percentage is that?
questions.shortAnswer: It is 60 percent: 18 divided by 30, multiplied by 100.
questions.answer: It is 60 percent: 18 divided by 30, multiplied by 100. State the sample and what daily use means.
keyPoints: It is 60 percent: 18 divided by 30, multiplied by 100.
State the sample and what daily use means.

topics.title: Central tendency and spread
topics.core: Mean, median and mode describe central tendency; range and standard deviation describe spread.
topics.explanation: The mean uses all values, the median is the sorted middle, and the mode is most frequent. Standard deviation summarises dispersion around the mean.
topics.example: For 2, 4, 4, 6: mean 4, median 4, mode 4 and range 4.
topics.confusion: Two groups with equal means can have very different distributions.

questions.prompt: Explain central tendency and spread briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Mean, median and mode describe central tendency; range and standard deviation describe spread.
questions.answer: Mean, median and mode describe central tendency; range and standard deviation describe spread. The mean uses all values, the median is the sorted middle, and the mode is most frequent.
keyPoints: Mean, median and mode describe central tendency; range and standard deviation describe spread.

questions.prompt: Why report standard deviation alongside a mean speaking score?
questions.shortAnswer: The mean gives the centre but not how varied learners are.
questions.answer: The mean gives the centre but not how varied learners are. Standard deviation helps describe the spread and prevents equal means from hiding different patterns.
keyPoints: The mean gives the centre but not how varied learners are.
Standard deviation helps describe the spread and prevents equal means from hiding different patterns.

topics.title: Chi-square
topics.core: A chi-square test of independence assesses association between categorical variables using observed and expected counts.
topics.explanation: The test compares counts with those expected under independence. Use a suitable contingency table and check expected-count and independence assumptions.
topics.example: Test whether preferred feedback type is associated with year of study.
topics.confusion: A significant association does not establish causation or its strength by itself.

questions.prompt: What is chi-square?
questions.shortAnswer: A chi-square test of independence assesses association between categorical variables using observed and expected counts.
questions.answer: A chi-square test of independence assesses association between categorical variables using observed and expected counts. The test compares counts with those expected under independence.
keyPoints: A chi-square test of independence assesses association between categorical variables using observed and expected counts.

questions.prompt: Would chi-square normally compare two mean fluency scores?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. A chi-square independence test is for categorical counts. A comparison of means requires an appropriate mean-comparison procedure and its assumptions.
keyPoints: No.
A chi-square independence test is for categorical counts.
A comparison of means requires an appropriate mean-comparison procedure and its assumptions.

topics.title: Pearson correlation
topics.core: Pearson's r measures the direction and strength of a linear relationship between two quantitative variables.
topics.explanation: It ranges from minus one to plus one. Zero indicates no linear association, not necessarily no relationship. Outliers and nonlinearity can make a summary misleading.
topics.example: A negative relationship could link higher anxiety scores with lower participation counts.
topics.confusion: Correlation does not by itself show that one variable causes another.

questions.prompt: What is pearson correlation?
questions.shortAnswer: Pearson's r measures the direction and strength of a linear relationship between two quantitative variables.
questions.answer: Pearson's r measures the direction and strength of a linear relationship between two quantitative variables. It ranges from minus one to plus one.
keyPoints: Pearson's r measures the direction and strength of a linear relationship between two quantitative variables.

questions.prompt: If r is zero, must two variables be unrelated?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. There may be a nonlinear relationship. Inspect the pattern and the measurement context instead of treating zero correlation as proof of complete independence.
keyPoints: No.
There may be a nonlinear relationship.
Inspect the pattern and the measurement context instead of treating zero correlation as proof of complete independence.

topics.title: Z-tests and t-tests
topics.core: A z-test uses the standard normal reference distribution; a t-test for a mean uses a t distribution when population variation is estimated.
topics.explanation: For the classic one-sample mean z-test, the population standard deviation is known and other distributional conditions must hold. A t-test uses sample variation. Test selection is not determined by sample size alone.
topics.example: Use a paired t-test to examine within-person pretest–posttest differences when its assumptions fit.
topics.confusion: A sample above 30 does not automatically require a z-test.

questions.prompt: Explain z-tests and t-tests briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A z-test uses the standard normal reference distribution; a t-test for a mean uses a t distribution when population variation is estimated.
questions.answer: A z-test uses the standard normal reference distribution; a t-test for a mean uses a t distribution when population variation is estimated. For the classic one-sample mean z-test, the population standard deviation is known and other distributional conditions must hold.
keyPoints: A z-test uses the standard normal reference distribution; a t-test for a mean uses a t distribution when population variation is estimated.

questions.prompt: Would you use an independent or paired t-test for the same learners' pretest and posttest scores?
questions.shortAnswer: A paired t-test treats each learner's two scores as a matched pair and analyses the differences, assuming the difference scores meet the required conditions.
questions.answer: A paired t-test treats each learner's two scores as a matched pair and analyses the differences, assuming the difference scores meet the required conditions.
keyPoints: A paired t-test treats each learner's two scores as a matched pair and analyses the differences, assuming the difference scores meet the required conditions.

topics.title: Factor analysis
topics.core: Factor analysis models shared patterns among observed variables using a smaller number of latent factors.
topics.explanation: It can explore whether questionnaire items reflect underlying constructs. The number and interpretation of factors require evidence and theoretical judgment.
topics.example: An anxiety questionnaire may contain related items about communication apprehension and evaluation fears.
topics.confusion: A statistical factor is not automatically a proven psychological cause.

questions.prompt: Explain factor analysis briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Factor analysis models shared patterns among observed variables using a smaller number of latent factors.
questions.answer: Factor analysis models shared patterns among observed variables using a smaller number of latent factors. It can explore whether questionnaire items reflect underlying constructs.
keyPoints: Factor analysis models shared patterns among observed variables using a smaller number of latent factors.

questions.prompt: Why use factor analysis while developing a learner-attitude questionnaire?
questions.shortAnswer: To examine patterns of shared variation and whether items cluster into plausible underlying dimensions, while also considering theory and other validity evidence.
questions.answer: To examine patterns of shared variation and whether items cluster into plausible underlying dimensions, while also considering theory and other validity evidence.
keyPoints: To examine patterns of shared variation and whether items cluster into plausible underlying dimensions, while also considering theory and other validity evidence.

topics.title: Results and discussion
topics.core: Results present the evidence; discussion explains what the findings mean in relation to questions and prior research.
topics.explanation: Use tables, figures, extracts and clear prose as appropriate. Interpretation should address alternative explanations and limits, not simply repeat the numbers.
topics.example: Report an observed score change, then discuss its possible meaning and relation to earlier findings.
topics.confusion: Qualitative findings are results too; results are not only statistical tables.

questions.prompt: Explain results and discussion briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Results present the evidence; discussion explains what the findings mean in relation to questions and prior research.
questions.answer: Results present the evidence; discussion explains what the findings mean in relation to questions and prior research. Use tables, figures, extracts and clear prose as appropriate.
keyPoints: Results present the evidence; discussion explains what the findings mean in relation to questions and prior research.

questions.prompt: How does 'the mean increased by 15' differ from a discussion claim?
questions.shortAnswer: The first describes a result.
questions.answer: The first describes a result. Discussion explains its significance and possible reasons, compares it with prior work and considers whether the design supports a causal interpretation.
keyPoints: The first describes a result.
Discussion explains its significance and possible reasons, compares it with prior work and considers whether the design supports a causal interpretation.

topics.title: Inference and recommendations
topics.core: Inference draws conclusions from evidence; recommendations propose actions supported by those conclusions.
topics.explanation: Keep claims within the design, sample and measurement limits. Recommendations can address practice or future research and should specify the context in which they apply.
topics.example: A small local case may suggest testing a strategy in other settings before wider adoption.
topics.confusion: A promising local result is not a universal teaching prescription.

questions.prompt: Explain inference and recommendations briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Inference draws conclusions from evidence; recommendations propose actions supported by those conclusions.
questions.answer: Inference draws conclusions from evidence; recommendations propose actions supported by those conclusions. Keep claims within the design, sample and measurement limits.
keyPoints: Inference draws conclusions from evidence; recommendations propose actions supported by those conclusions.

questions.prompt: Can a study of one class justify a policy for every university?
questions.shortAnswer: Not by itself.
questions.answer: Not by itself. It can provide contextual insight and motivate broader investigation, but sweeping recommendations exceed the evidence's scope.
keyPoints: Not by itself.
It can provide contextual insight and motivate broader investigation, but sweeping recommendations exceed the evidence's scope.

topics.title: Citation and plagiarism
topics.core: Citation credits borrowed ideas and words; plagiarism presents another person's work as one's own.
topics.explanation: A genuine paraphrase changes the structure and wording while retaining the meaning and citing the source. Exact wording requires quotation treatment and a locator.
topics.example: After explaining an author's idea in your own words, include author and year and a matching reference.
topics.confusion: Changing a few words does not turn copied structure into an adequate paraphrase.

questions.prompt: Explain citation and plagiarism briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: Citation credits borrowed ideas and words; plagiarism presents another person's work as one's own.
questions.answer: Citation credits borrowed ideas and words; plagiarism presents another person's work as one's own. A genuine paraphrase changes the structure and wording while retaining the meaning and citing the source.
keyPoints: Citation credits borrowed ideas and words; plagiarism presents another person's work as one's own.

questions.prompt: Does paraphrasing remove the need for a citation?
questions.shortAnswer: No.
questions.answer: No. The idea still comes from a source. Credit the author and year even when using your own wording.
keyPoints: No.
The idea still comes from a source.
Credit the author and year even when using your own wording.

topics.title: APA in-text citation and quotation
topics.core: APA uses author–date in-text citations linked to entries in a reference list.
topics.explanation: Ordinary three-or-more-author in-text citations use the first surname and et al. Direct quotations need a page or other suitable locator. Quotations of 40 words or more use block format.
topics.example: A fictional example is (Rahman et al., 2024); a quotation might add p. 12.
topics.confusion: The reference list uses full author details under APA rules, not ordinary in-text et al. shortening.

questions.prompt: Explain apa in-text citation and quotation briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: APA uses author–date in-text citations linked to entries in a reference list.
questions.answer: APA uses author–date in-text citations linked to entries in a reference list. Ordinary three-or-more-author in-text citations use the first surname and et al.
