keyPoints: APA uses author–date in-text citations linked to entries in a reference list.

questions.prompt: What extra information does a direct quotation need compared with an ordinary paraphrase?
questions.shortAnswer: It needs quotation formatting and a specific locator such as a page number, as well as the author and year.
questions.answer: It needs quotation formatting and a specific locator such as a page number, as well as the author and year. A locator is optional but often useful for a paraphrase.
keyPoints: It needs quotation formatting and a specific locator such as a page number, as well as the author and year.
A locator is optional but often useful for a paraphrase.

topics.title: APA reference entries
topics.core: A reference entry identifies a source through its author, date, title and publication information.
topics.explanation: Identify the source type first. Books, journal articles and chapters require different arrangements. APA 7 omits a publisher's city and presents available DOIs as URLs.
topics.example: A chapter entry starts with its chapter author, then identifies the editor and book.
topics.confusion: Do not invent missing dates, page ranges, journals or DOIs to fill a format.

questions.prompt: Explain apa reference entries briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A reference entry identifies a source through its author, date, title and publication information.
questions.answer: A reference entry identifies a source through its author, date, title and publication information. Identify the source type first.
keyPoints: A reference entry identifies a source through its author, date, title and publication information.

questions.prompt: Who appears first in an APA reference for a chapter in an edited book?
questions.shortAnswer: The chapter author.
questions.answer: The chapter author. The editor appears later with the book information because the specific cited contribution is the chapter.
keyPoints: The chapter author.
The editor appears later with the book information because the specific cited contribution is the chapter.

topics.title: Research proposals and frameworks
topics.core: A proposal explains what a study plans to investigate, why it matters and how it will be conducted.
topics.explanation: Include the problem, literature, questions, framework, methods, ethics, expected contribution, timeline and references. A theoretical framework draws on theory; a conceptual framework specifies the study's concepts and relationships.
topics.example: Plan a study of role-play and fluency with participants, measures, comparison and analysis.
topics.confusion: A proposal must not present invented results as if the study has happened.

questions.prompt: Explain research proposals and frameworks briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A proposal explains what a study plans to investigate, why it matters and how it will be conducted.
questions.answer: A proposal explains what a study plans to investigate, why it matters and how it will be conducted. Include the problem, literature, questions, framework, methods, ethics, expected contribution, timeline and references.
keyPoints: A proposal explains what a study plans to investigate, why it matters and how it will be conducted.

questions.prompt: What should a proposal say about findings before data are collected?
questions.shortAnswer: It may state hypotheses or expected contributions, clearly as expectations.
questions.answer: It may state hypotheses or expected contributions, clearly as expectations. It must not fabricate findings; it should explain how the eventual evidence will answer the questions.
keyPoints: It may state hypotheses or expected contributions, clearly as expectations.
It must not fabricate findings; it should explain how the eventual evidence will answer the questions.

topics.title: Research papers and dissertations
topics.core: A research report explains the question, methods, evidence and reasoned conclusions of a completed study.
topics.explanation: A common dissertation structure includes introduction, literature review, methodology, results, discussion and conclusion. Articles often compress these functions; requirements vary by discipline and venue.
topics.example: A report connects its discussion back to the research questions and ends with implications and limits.
topics.confusion: An abstract summarises the whole study rather than serving as another general introduction.

questions.prompt: Explain research papers and dissertations briefly.
questions.shortAnswer: A research report explains the question, methods, evidence and reasoned conclusions of a completed study.
questions.answer: A research report explains the question, methods, evidence and reasoned conclusions of a completed study. A common dissertation structure includes introduction, literature review, methodology, results, discussion and conclusion.
keyPoints: A research report explains the question, methods, evidence and reasoned conclusions of a completed study.

questions.prompt: What should a concise research-article abstract normally cover?
questions.shortAnswer: The problem or purpose, the main methods, central findings and conclusion or implication.
questions.answer: The problem or purpose, the main methods, central findings and conclusion or implication. For a proposal, describe planned work and omit invented findings.
keyPoints: The problem or purpose, the main methods, central findings and conclusion or implication.
For a proposal, describe planned work and omit invented findings.
